title: Why Companies Keep Getting Personality Tests, OKRs, and Growth Mindset Backward
author: Nir Eyal and Jasmine Eyal
summary: Nir and Jasmine Eyal argue that management practices fail in two ways: through neglect, where people skip the process, and through full reversal, where the practice is used in a way that undermines its own purpose. They examine three popular tools. OKRs become defensive when stretch goals are tied to bonuses, growth mindset becomes wall-poster branding or a justification for escalating commitment to failing projects, and personality assessments lose their predictive signal once they become high-stakes hiring gates. Each claim is backed by recent studies, including a 2026 lab experiment on goal-setting bonuses, a 2022 analysis of 8,775 students and 223 teachers, and a 2025 meta-analysis showing validity falling from .27 to .12 in high-stakes settings. The repair advice is concrete: label commitments separately from stretch goals, align promotions and feedback with stated learning values, and validate any assessment against the actual role. The closing test for any leader is whether the practice still produces the outcome it was meant to create.
points: Reversal is more dangerous than neglect because leaders can cite a score or process they believe they are running correctly while using it backward.
Tying stretch-goal OKRs to compensation turns an experiment into a promise, so teams protect themselves and set safer targets instead of stretching.

Growth mindset only works inside a supportive context: a randomized school intervention helped students only when their teachers also endorsed growth beliefs, and the workplace parallel is that managers must make mistakes safe.
Personality tests used as hiring gates lose predictive power because high-stakes applicants answer for what the employer wants, and AI-polished responses make this worse.
Leaders should separate commitments from stretch goals, reward learning in promotions and reviews, and combine assessments with structured interviews and work samples.
quotes: There are two ways this happens. The obvious failure is neglect: People skip the process or adopt the tool halfway. But the more dangerous failure is full reversal: People use the practice in a way that undermines the purpose it was designed to serve.
Reversal is more pernicious and harder to notice. Leaders can point to a score or process they believe they are implementing correctly while unknowingly using it backward.
But a stretch goal should create permission to attempt something whose outcome is uncertain. Making a bonus mechanically depend on achieving it converts an experiment into a promise.
Many organizations copy growth mindset by writing ‘growth mindset’ on the walls and doing little else, and that doesn’t work.
The study took place in schools, but the workplace parallel is straightforward. A company cannot credibly ask employees to learn from mistakes when managers make mistakes unsafe.

The reversal occurs when the assessment becomes a gate. Once applicants know their answers may determine whether a human ever sees their application, the score begins to reflect how well candidates can infer what the employer wants.

Automation makes it easy to turn a score into a cutoff and reject applicants before anyone weighs their experience, work samples, or circumstances. But faster rejection is not necessarily better selection.
Leaders should ask a simple question before adopting the next practice: Does the way we are using this tool still produce the outcome it was meant to create?
